newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BoE monetary committee shows its colours.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BoE monetary committee shows its colours.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, showing its colours for the first time on Wednesday, said it expected British inflation to continue to rise because of robust economic growth.

Minutes of the committee's first meeting on June 6 showed all of its members, including outsiders nominated by the new Labour government, voted in favour of raising official interest rates to 6.5 percent from 6.25 percent.
The committee, chaired by Bank of England governor Eddie George, raised rates again to 6.75 percent at its subsequent monthly meeting last week.
"Taking account of the outlook for both domestic and external demand, total output was likely to continue growing at above-trend rates," the minutes said.

"Members agreed that the prospect for domestic demand was sufficiently buoyant that, despite the probable future impact of the higher exchange rate on activity, there was a need for tighter monetary policy in order to hit the inflation target looking two years or so ahead."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown stunned financial markets within days of Labour's May 1 landslide election victory by ceding one of his key powers -- the right to set interest rates -- to the new committee.
The committee must set policy to meet the 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation set by the government. Underlying inflation rose to 2.7 percent in June from 2.5 percent in May.

The minutes showed members paid considerable attention to the damage the soaring pound is inflicting on British exporters, but concluded that this was no justification for delaying a rise in interest rates to slow domestic demand.
"Basically, they made clear that the inflation target is the key," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International.

"They are going to tighten policy to achieve the inflation target, even if as a by-product of this, the strong pound causes damage to some sections of the economy. I felt there was a bias towards raising rates."
James KcKay, an economist at PaineWebber, said the central bank appeared to be paying more attention to the exchange rate than it had in the past.

"However, I suspect the Bank of England may try to be rather hawkish against inflationary pressure," he said. "I believe that with a newly independent central bank, the risks are for a tighter monetary policy than absolutely necessary."

A compilation of independent economic forecasts published by the Treasury on Wednesday showed an average forecast for interest rates of 7.23 percent in the last quarter of this year and 7.47 percent at the end of 1998.
Some economists were disappointed that the views of individual members of the committee were not outlined in the minutes.
"Throughout, the committee speaks with one voice," said Geoffrey Dicks of NatWest Markets. "No individual contributions are identified. It is hard even to distinguish any shades of opinion."
But David Mackie, an economist at JP Morgan in London, said Britain's monetary policy framework was among the most open and transparent in the world.

"Only if you are really familiar with other countries are you aware just how secretive most central banks are," he said. "To expect named contributions in the discussion in the monetary policy committee is probably a bit unrealistic."
However, economists said the committee's conclusion that higher interest rates were needed at the moment was uncontroversial and differences of opinion could become apparent after future meetings.
"That would be useful as we could build up profiles similar to those for Federal Reserve governors in the U.S., where some are regarded as inflation hawks and some as doves," McKay said.
